title: Break-even analysis with a worked calculation for residential cleaning
audience: Owners of residential cleaning businesses, including solo operators, who set prices or plan monthly income from regular and one-off house cleans.
learningOutcomes: Classify the costs of a home-service business as fixed or variable
Calculate monthly break-even revenue from fixed costs and a variable cost percentage
Explain why conflicting break-even figures must be reconciled before any of them is used

instruction.heading: What break-even means for a house cleaner
instruction.body: Break-even revenue is the monthly sales that cover all costs, so profit is zero. For a house cleaner it shows how many cleans must run each month before any profit is made. ANZ defines fixed and variable costs and warns that costs must be covered to avoid running at a loss. The figure is only as good as the costs that go into it.

instruction.heading: Split the costs for a house cleaning business
instruction.body: Fixed costs stay the same whatever the number of cleans: vehicle registration and loan repayments, insurance, phone and software, and any storage space. Variable costs move with each clean: chemicals and cloths used on the job, bin liners, card and payment fees and any casual cleaner's hours. A casual cleaner paid by the hour has wages that rise with the work, so treat those wages as variable and include them in the variable share. If you leave them out, break-even looks too low. Express variable cost as a share of sales for the same months, and check that share over several months before you rely on it.

instruction.heading: The formula
instruction.body: Break-even revenue equals fixed costs divided by one minus the variable share of sales. The result after variable cost is the contribution margin: the part of each dollar of sales that is left to cover fixed costs (Xero Australia glossary, 23 July 2026). The formula gives revenue, not profit. To convert it into cleans, divide by your average price actually charged per clean, and round up to whole cleans, because a part clean does not cover costs.

instruction.heading: Work the calculation in order
instruction.body: Write each input with its period and source. Compute the contribution margin, divide the fixed costs by it, then divide the answer by the average price per clean. The average price must be the price you actually charged after any discount. A marketplace range is a reference, not an input: its regular-clean range is $80 to $180 (Airtasker, Airbnb cleaning page, 27 August 2025).

instruction.heading: Reconcile two figures before you use either
instruction.body: When two figures disagree, check whether fixed costs are monthly or annual, whether the variable percentage is a share of sales or of cost, and whether the output is revenue or profit. Keep only the reconciled figure, with its inputs. A break-even figure whose inputs you cannot see should not be used to set a price. The research did not find Australian cost ratios for residential cleaning, so every input here must come from your own records.

procedure: List every monthly cost for the cleaning business and label each one fixed or variable.
Count any casual cleaner's wages as variable, along with chemicals, bin liners and payment fees.
Work out variable cost as a share of sales for the same months, and check it across several months.
Calculate one minus the variable share to find the contribution margin, then divide monthly fixed costs by it.
Divide break-even revenue by the average price actually charged per clean, and round up to whole cleans.
Compare any other figure, reconcile the inputs, and keep only the reconciled one.

workedExamples.situation: A solo house cleaner (illustrative) charges an average of $240 a clean, based on a two-bedroom home at $120 an hour for two hours. The $120 is the Airtasker reference for two bedrooms (27 August 2025), and the two hours are illustrative. Fixed costs are $2,400 a month and variable costs are 18 per cent of sales, both illustrative. The owner works alone and has no casual cleaner.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How many cleans must be done each month to break even, and what changes if a casual cleaner is hired?
workedExamples.reasoning: The contribution margin is 1 - 0.18, which is 0.82. Break-even revenue is $2,400 divided by 0.82, which is $2,926.83 a month (CALC). At $240 a clean that is 12.2 cleans, so 13 are needed. Check: 12 cleans give $2,361.60 of contribution, which is short of $2,400, and 13 give $2,558.40. If a casual cleaner is hired at the award floor of $32.31 an hour for two hours, the wage is $64.62 per clean. That is 26.93 per cent of $240 (CALC). The variable share becomes 44.93 per cent, the contribution margin 0.5508, and break-even $4,357.69 a month, which is 19 cleans. The award floor excludes on-costs, so the true figure is higher. The hiring decision must use the full variable cost.

equipmentAndPpe: Cost list for the last three months

commonErrors.error: Treating a casual cleaner's hours as a fixed cost.
commonErrors.prevention: Track their hours per clean. Because they move with the work, include them in the variable share.

commonErrors.error: Using variable cost as a share of cost instead of a share of sales.
commonErrors.prevention: Divide by sales for the same months, and write the denominator beside the percentage.

commonErrors.error: Using a marketplace price as the average price per clean.
commonErrors.prevention: Use the price you actually charged after discounts. The marketplace range is a reference only.

commonErrors.error: Copying a break-even figure from a blog or a plan without its inputs.
commonErrors.prevention: Recalculate with your own inputs and record the source and date of each one.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Business planning only. This lesson gives no tax or accounting advice. Check how your costs and any wages are treated with a registered tax agent or accountant. The research did not confirm the tax treatment.

The wage in the example is the Cleaning Services Award Level 1 adult minimum of $25.85 an hour with a 25 per cent casual loading, from 1 July 2025 (Fair Work Commission). The 2026-27 rates were not checked.

qualityStandard: Every break-even figure shows its fixed costs, variable percentage, period and source.
Two figures that disagree are reconciled before either one is used in a plan or a price.
documentationEvidence: Cost list split into fixed and variable, with source and date
Reconciliation note wherever two figures disagree
summary: Break-even revenue is fixed costs divided by one minus the variable share of sales.
If you hire casual cleaners, their wages are variable. Include them before you set a target.
Gap: no Australian source for residential cleaning cost ratios was found. Every input in this lesson is illustrative and must come from your own records.

knowledgeChecks.question: Break-even revenue for a house cleaning business is calculated as:
options: Fixed costs multiplied by the variable percentage
Fixed costs divided by (1 minus the variable share of sales)
Sales minus fixed costs, shown as a percentage of the price
Fixed costs plus variable costs for the month

knowledgeChecks.question: Fixed costs are $2,400 a month, variable costs are 18 per cent of sales, and an average clean is $240. What is the monthly break-even revenue?
A casual cleaner is hired by the hour and works two hours per clean. Why must those wages change the break-even target?
options: Because the wages move with each clean, so they belong in variable costs
Because wages are always fixed costs, whatever the work
Because wages do not affect break-even at all
Because the wages are paid to the household, not the cleaner

sourceReferences: ANZ, 'Setting the right price for your product or service', https://www.anz.com.au/business/business-hub/starting-business/start/setting-the-right-price-for-your-product-or-service/, dated 21 February 2025, last modified 22 July 2025. Supports: definitions of fixed and variable costs; costs must be covered to avoid running at a loss.

Xero Australia, 'Break-even point formula' glossary entry, https://www.xero.com/au/glossary/break-even-point-formula/, dated 23 July 2026. Supports: contribution margin is price minus variable cost; break-even revenue is fixed costs divided by the contribution ratio; job counts are rounded up to whole jobs.

Airtasker, 'Airbnb cleaning service cost', https://www.airtasker.com/au/costs/airbnb-cleaning/airbnb-cleaning-service-cost, last updated 27 August 2025. Vendor marketplace; the house-cleaning page could not be read. Supports: hourly rates by bedroom count, per-room prices, a regular clean range of $80 to $180, and a guest fee range of $50 to $300 per booking.

Fair Work Commission, Cleaning Services Award (MA000022), https://awards.fairwork.gov.au/MA000022.html, variation effective 1 July 2025. Supports: Level 1 adult minimum hourly rate of $25.85 and a 25 per cent casual loading. The 1 July 2026 position was not checked.
Notes: the $2,400 fixed costs, 18 per cent variable share, $240 average clean and two-hour job are illustrative and not market data. Figures marked CALC are arithmetic on those inputs.
